Trail **#1095** — its description predates the last two rounds (no case-fold fix, no measurements). Here's updated text. I haven't posted it; paste or tell me to apply it with `entire trail update`.

```
Problem:
redaction.openai_privacy_filter.command becomes argv[0] of an exec during the
pre-push OPF rewrite, and it was read from the version-controlled
.entire/settings.json with no validation. A pull request could commit a payload
and a settings file naming it; pushing executed it. A JSON settings diff does
not read as executable to a reviewer, and nothing stood in the way: the prompt
never names the command, prompt_default "always" skips it, and non-TTY pushes
(CI, agent-driven) auto-run. Execution happened before any failure handling, so
a payload exiting 0 with valid JSON left no warning.

Two further problems surfaced while fixing it:
- logging.Init called its log-level getter (which loads settings, which logs)
  while holding a non-reentrant write lock. Any log call from the loader hung
  the process. Latent before this work; the new diagnostic triggered it.
- The tracked-path check compared paths exactly. On case-insensitive volumes
  (macOS/Windows default) a PR committing .entire/Settings.Local.json is
  materialized by checkout, opened by readConfined under the canonical name,
  and missed by the lookup — read as settings while judged untracked. Reported
  by Cursor Bugbot on #2056.

Solution:
Gate on ownership, not syntax — a path is legitimate for anyone whose opf
binary is not on $PATH.

- command is honored only from .entire/settings.local.json, verified untracked.
- A tracked settings.local.json is ignored wholesale. .gitignore does not apply
  to an already-tracked path, so `git add -f` commits it and a clone
  materializes it with the committer's content, overriding project settings for
  everyone.
- Rejection never fails the load; one committed file must not brick status and
  doctor. The loader records the reason, consumers report it on stderr, and
  `entire status --detailed` marks an ignored layer instead of rendering it live.
- Path matching folds case on both sides; object.Tree.FindEntry matches
  exactly, so the HEAD walk is explicit per component.

Two deliberate asymmetries:
- Failure direction. An unverifiable repo keeps the layer (losing every local
  preference is worse than the risk) but drops the exec-bearing command (being
  wrong means running someone else's binary). No repo at all is proof of
  locality.
- Check depth. The layer check reads the index; command also reads HEAD. A PR
  puts the file in the index of every clone that checks it out, and checkout
  cannot produce a file absent from the index, so "committed then git rm
  --cached" is a locally created state. HEAD is the expensive half: skipping it
  measures 8.3ms -> 2.5ms per hook process, 39ms -> 11ms on reftable.

logging.Init now resolves the level before taking its lock, which also makes
the two pre-existing logging.Debug calls in settings.Load safe.

Verification: attack reproduced end-to-end before and after (payload executes
pre-fix, does not post-fix), including the case-variant path on a
case-insensitive volume; deadlock confirmed by stack dump and pinned by a test
that hangs without the fix. 22 unit + 3 integration tests, the integration ones
running the real binary through real git hooks with a positive control (same
payload via an untracked local file does execute), so a negative result cannot
pass vacuously.

Follow-ups not in this PR: agent/registry.go:34-43,65 has the same
callback-under-lock shape plus a recursive RLock; setup.go:650 writes a merged
struct into a scoped settings file, which that file's own comment forbids.
```

content.text:
**Yes — a `command` in `.entire/settings.json` never reaches exec on its own.** I ran the full matrix rather than answering from memory:

| project sets `command` + … | effective | rejected |
|---|---|---|
| no local file | `""` | yes |
| local file exists, no `command` key | `""` | yes |
| local file is tracked | `""` | yes |
| local sets a *different* command (untracked) | local's value | no |
| local sets the *same* string (untracked) | that value | no |

The first three are the ones you're asking about: ignored in every case, falling back to `opf` on `$PATH`.

**The nuance** is the last row. The gate keys on *who chose the value*, not *what the value is* — so if a developer independently writes the same string in their own untracked `settings.local.json`, it's honored. That's correct rather than a hole: an attacker committing `command: X` still cannot make X run; only a local declaration can, and at that point the developer chose it. The project file's value is also simply overwritten by the merge in that case, so it's never "the project's value being honored" — it's the local one that happens to match.

Row 2 was the one I'd call load-bearing and it wasn't covered: a developer with a local file for *unrelated* settings (say `commit_linking`) must not thereby legitimize a committed command. Provenance is per-key, not per-file — verified, and now pinned by a test. Row 5 is pinned too, since a refactor could plausibly flip those two in opposite directions.

Pushed as `dff119fd6`. Five commits, lint and `test:ci` green.

ok, two more findings:

1:

Real latent bug: first-match-wins descent (Linux-relevant)

This is the concrete answer to your question. treeHasPathFold descends into the first fold-matching entry and breaks:

for j := range current.Entries {
    if pathsEqualFold(current.Entries[j].Name, part) {
        match = &current.Entries[j]
        break            // first fold-match wins
    }
}
...
sub, err := current.Tree(match.Name)  // descends into that one only

Git objects are case-sensitive, so a tree can legitimately hold both .Entire/ and .entire/ as distinct entries (and git sorts uppercase before lowercase, so .Entire is visited first). If the first fold-matching entry is the wrong one — a directory lacking the child, or a blob named .Entire (→ current.Tree returns ErrDirectoryNotFound → false) — the walk returns a false negative and never checks the sibling .entire/ that actually contains the file.

This is asymmetric with the index side, which scans all entries and returns true on any match ("any fold-variant is tracked" — the correct semantics). The tree walk instead answers "the first-fold-matching chain contains it."

Severity: low, and not a reachable bypass, because:
- For PR delivery, the file is always in the index (checkout populatebeLocalSettingsIsVersioned checks the index first and returns true
there — treeHasPathFold is never consulted.
- The HEAD/tree path runs only when the file is index-absent-but-HEADed — a state the victim created locally, not one a PR can deliver (the
PR's own rationale for why HEAD is the belt, not the suspenders).

But it's a genuine correctness inconsistency in a security predicate, and it bites the moment the tree walk is reused somewhere HEAD is authoritative, or if the index
short-circuit is ever refactored. It affects Linux (and any case-sensws victim) at the git-object level; it can't arise from two on-disksiblings on a case-insensitive FS.

Suggested fix: don't break on the first fold-match. Either collect alach level and DFS into each, or for the terminal component check "anyentry folds," mirroring the index scan's "any match" semantics. A regtaining both .Entire/ (decoy, no child or a blob) and.entire/settings.local.json (real) would fail today.

2: 

NTFS (Windows): yes — plausible, PR-deliverable bypass

Win32 silently strips trailing dots and spaces from filenames. This is a pure-ASCII, non-case equivalence, and it is exactly the class core.protectNTFS exists to defend — but core.protectNTFS only guards .git-family names, not .entire/settings.local.json.

Attack:
1. PR commits .entire/settings.local.json. (trailing dot) — or ...json  (trailing space) — with a malicious command, plus the payload.
2. On a Windows clone, git checks the entry out; Win32 strips the trailing dot, so the working-tree file is .entire/settings.local.json (the canonical name).
3. readConfined("settings.local.json") opens it → the attacker's command becomes the effective local override.
4. The trust check scans index/HEAD and compares with strings.EqualFold(".entire/settings.local.json.", ".entire/settings.local.json") → false (trailing .). Verdict: untracked → localOwn → command executed. RCE.

Critically, this defeats the index check — the authoritative one for PR delivery — not just the HEAD "belt." So unlike the treeHasPathFold first-match issue, this one is reachable by a pure pull request.

One dependency to confirm with a real Windows repro: the attack requires that git-for-Windows materializes the checked-out file under the canonical (stripped) name (standard CreateFileW behavior — very likely) rather than writing the literal trailing-dot name via a \\?\ extended path. If git wrote the literal name, os.Root.Open("settings.local.json") would miss it and the attack fizzles. Given git-for-Windows's long history with core.protectNTFS precisely because Win32 stripping is the default, I rate this likely reachable — moderate-to-high severity, pending the repro. Trailing space behaves identically.

(Other NTFS tricks I checked and dismissed: ADS ::$DATA is a read-side suffix, not a commit-side name, and readConfined opens the bare base name, so it isn't invoked; 8.3 short names are FS-generated aliases for long names, not the reverse, so committing SETTIN~1.JSO doesn't make settings.local.json resolve to it.)
Both are worth taking seriously. Let me read the current implementation.
